claim: The auto-inhibited, super-relaxed (SRX) state of cardiac myosin is thought to be crucial for regulating contraction, relaxation, and energy conservation in the heart.
source: The auto-inhibited, super-relaxed (SRX) state of cardiac myosin is thought to be crucial for regulating contraction, relaxation, and energy conservation in the heart.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing the importance of the SRX state.

claim: The E525K dilated cardiomyopathy mutation in human beta-cardiac myosin increases the fraction of myosin heads in the SRX state, especially in physiological ionic strength conditions.
source: We used single ATP turnover experiments to demonstrate that a dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) mutation (E525K) in human beta-cardiac myosin increases the fraction of myosin heads in the SRX state (with slow ATP turnover), especially in physiological ionic strength conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by single ATP turnover experiments presented in the manuscript (Figure 3).

claim: There is a strong correlation between the interacting-heads motif (IHM) and the SRX state in cardiac myosin.
source: We also utilized FRET between a C-terminal GFP tag on the myosin tail and Cy3ATP bound to the active site of the motor domain to estimate the fraction of heads in the closed, interacting-heads motif (IHM); we found a strong correlation between the IHM and SRX state.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET experiments and their correlation with single turnover measurements (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The E525K mutation increased the fraction of molecules adopting the IHM as demonstrated by negative stain electron microscopy and 2D class averaging.
source: Negative stain electron microscopy and 2D class averaging of the construct demonstrated that the E525K mutation increased the fraction of molecules adopting the IHM.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data and 2D class averaging presented in Figure 6.

claim: The E525K DCM mutation may reduce muscle force and power by stabilizing the auto-inhibited SRX state.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that the E525K DCM mutation may reduce muscle force and power by stabilizing the auto-inhibited SRX state.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing increased SRX state in the mutant.

claim: Myosin heads in the thick filament can fold back on the myosin tail and interact with each other in a conformation referred to as the interacting-heads motif (IHM).
source: Structural studies have shown that myosin heads in the thick filament can fold back on the myosin tail and interact with each other in a conformation referred to as the interacting-heads motif (IHM; Alamo et al., 2018; Woodhead et al., 2005; Zoghbi et al., 2008), which prevents them from interacting with actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The IHM prevents myosin heads from interacting with actin.
source: Structural studies have shown that myosin heads in the thick filament can fold back on the myosin tail and interact with each other in a conformation referred to as the interacting-heads motif (IHM; Alamo et al., 2018; Woodhead et al., 2005; Zoghbi et al., 2008), which prevents them from interacting with actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: It is currently unclear if the SRX biochemical state and IHM structural state are directly correlated.
source: However, it is currently unclear if the SRX biochemical state and IHM structural state are directly correlated (Craig and Padrón, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation indicating the uncertainty in the field.

claim: SRX heads turn over ATP about 5–10 times slower than the uninhibited disordered relaxed (DRX) heads.
source: It appears to play a crucial role in conserving energy, as SRX heads turn over ATP about 5–10 times slower than the uninhibited disordered relaxed (DRX) heads (Hooijman et al., 2011; Toepfer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies measuring ATP turnover rates.

claim: Cardiac muscle may use the SRX heads as a reserve that can be recruited when peripheral metabolic demands warrant increased cardiac contractility.
source: Cardiac muscle may also use the SRX heads as a reserve that can be recruited when peripheral metabolic demands warrant-increased cardiac contractility (McNamara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Regulation of the SRX state in cardiac muscle may underlie the Frank-Starling mechanism.
source: It has been hypothesized that regulation of the SRX state in cardiac muscle underlies the Frank-Starling mechanism, in which contractile force increases as cardiac muscle is stretched (i.e. length-dependent activation; Campbell et al., 2018; Kampourakis and Irving, 2021; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies proposing this hypothesis.

claim: Several HCM mutations in cardiac myosin can destabilize the SRX state.
source: Recent work has revealed that several HCM mutations in cardiac myosin can destabilize the SRX state (Adhikari et al., 2019; Anderson et al., 2018; Gollapudi et al., 2021; Sarkar et al., 2020; Vander Roest et al., 2021), which may explain the impaired relaxation and hypercontractile phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Destabilization of the SRX state by HCM mutations may explain the impaired relaxation and hypercontractile phenotype.
source: Recent work has revealed that several HCM mutations in cardiac myosin can destabilize the SRX state (Adhikari et al., 2019; Anderson et al., 2018; Gollapudi et al., 2021; Sarkar et al., 2020; Vander Roest et al., 2021), which may explain the impaired relaxation and hypercontractile phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited studies.

claim: DCM presents as an increase in left ventricular chamber size which leads to thinning of the myocardium, cardiomyocyte cell death, and a hypocontractile phenotype.
source: On the other hand, DCM presents as an increase in left ventricular chamber size which leads to thinning of the myocardium, cardiomyocyte cell death, and a hypocontractile phenotype (McNally and Mestroni, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study describing DCM characteristics.

claim: Early-stage DCM patients present with subtle decreases in contractility and ejection fraction, suggesting hypocontractility may trigger disease onset.
source: Interestingly, early-stage DCM patients present with subtle decreases in contractility and ejection fraction, suggesting hypocontractility may trigger disease onset (Lakdawala et al., 2012b; Schafer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: DCM mutations may stabilize the SRX state, which reduces the number of myosin heads available to produce contractile force and could explain the observed hypocontractility.
source: An attractive hypothesis is that DCM mutations may stabilize the SRX state, which reduces the number of myosin heads available to produce contractile force and could explain the observed hypocontractility.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on reasoning.

claim: The leading hypothesis is that DCM mutations reduce the intrinsic motor properties of myosin without altering the SRX state.
source: However, the leading hypothesis is that DCM mutations reduce the intrinsic motor properties of myosin without altering the SRX state (Robert-Paganin et al., 2018; Ujfalusi et al., 2018), although few studies have examined the impact of DCM mutations on the SRX state (Yuan et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The IHM has been proposed to be the structural basis of the SRX state.
source: The IHM, which appears to be a conserved regulatory structure in all muscle types (Alamo et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018), has been proposed to be the structural basis of the SRX state (Craig and Padrón, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The IHM is a conserved regulatory structure in all muscle types.
source: The IHM, which appears to be a conserved regulatory structure in all muscle types (Alamo et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018), has been proposed to be the structural basis of the SRX state (Craig and Padrón, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The IHM is found in both single myosin molecules and native thick filaments.
source: The motif is found in both single myosin molecules and native thick filaments.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Early studies with smooth and non-muscle myosin revealed a folded tail conformation that was proposed to be auto-inhibitory.
source: Early studies with smooth and non-muscle myosin revealed a folded tail conformation that was proposed to be auto-inhibitory (Craig et al., 1983; Onishi and Wakabayashi, 1982; Trybus et al., 1982; Trybus and Lowey, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to early studies.

claim: A study with smooth muscle myosin was the first to reveal the interactions between the heads that characterize the IHM.
source: A study with smooth muscle myosin was the first to reveal the interactions between the heads that characterize the IHM (Wendt et al., 1999; Wendt et al., 2001) and later how the folded tail stabilizes the interacting heads (Burgess et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: The IHM has been demonstrated in myosin II molecules across the evolutionary tree, from humans to the earliest animals.
source: The motif subsequently has been demonstrated in myosin II molecules across the evolutionary tree, from humans to the earliest animals (e.g. sponges; Jung et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating evolutionary conservation.

claim: The IHM is the auto-inhibited structure that predominates in the dephosphorylated off-state.
source: Further biochemical studies demonstrated that the IHM is the auto-inhibited structure that predominates in the dephosphorylated off-state (Burgess et al., 2007; Cross et al., 1988; Wendt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: Three recent cryo-EM studies of smooth muscle myosin solved the high-resolution structure of the IHM.
source: Three recent cryo-EM studies of smooth muscle myosin solved the high-resolution structure of the IHM, providing crucial details about head-head and head-tail interactions that stabilize the structure (Heissler et al., 2021; Scarff et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent cryo-EM studies.

claim: The IHM was first demonstrated in native thick filaments in tarantula muscle.
source: The IHM was first demonstrated in native thick filaments in tarantula muscle (Woodhead et al., 2005) and then was shown to be conserved in thick filaments throughout the animal kingdom, including vertebrates (AlKhayat et al., 2013; Alamo et al., 2017; Zoghbi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The highest resolution IHM structure so far (13 Å) has come from tarantula filaments.
source: The highest resolution so far (13 Å) has come from tarantula filaments (Yang et al., 2016), which showed an IHM with similar features to smooth muscle myosin (Alamo et al., 2018; Alamo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: In skeletal and cardiac myosin, the high-resolution structure of the IHM has not been solved.
source: However, in skeletal and cardiac myosin, the high-resolution structure of the IHM has not been solved.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of the current state of the field.

claim: The authors developed a method of detecting the IHM in solution by FRET.
source: In the current study, we developed a method of detecting the IHM in solution by FRET, allowing us to directly correlate the fraction of myosin heads in the IHM with the fraction of myosin heads in the slow ATP turnover (SRX) state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors generated human beta-cardiac heavy meromyosin (HMM) with 15 heptads of S2, a leucine zipper, and a C-terminal GFP tag (M2β 15HPZ.GFP).
source: Thus, we generated human beta-cardiac heavy meromyosin (HMM) with 15 heptads of S2, a leucine zipper, and a C-terminal GFP tag (M2β 15HPZ.GFP; Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the construct in the methods and results.

claim: At least 15 heptads of the S2 region of myosin were required for phosphorylation-dependent regulation in smooth muscle myosin.
source: Previous studies in smooth muscle myosin demonstrated that at least 15 heptads of the S2 region of myosin were required for phosphorylation-dependent regulation (Trybus et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The M2β 15HPZ.GFP construct was expressed and purified using the C2C12 expression system.
source: We expressed and purified M2β 15HPZ.GFP using the C2C12 expression system (Chow et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2003), and the myosin contained endogenous mouse skeletal muscle light chains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods description and citations.

claim: The myosin contained endogenous mouse skeletal muscle light chains.
source: We expressed and purified M2β 15HPZ.GFP using the C2C12 expression system (Chow et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2003), and the myosin contained endogenous mouse skeletal muscle light chains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the methods description.

claim: If M2β 15HPZ.GFP forms the IHM, FRET should be observable between Cy3ATP bound to the active site and the C-terminal GFP tag.
source: We reasoned that if M2β 15HPZ.GFP forms the IHM then we should be able to observe FRET between Cy3ATP bound to the active site and the C-terminal GFP tag, thus essentially functioning as a biosensor of the IHM or closed state.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the FRET biosensor design.

claim: The predicted distance between the active site of the free head (FH) and its C-terminal GFP tag is about 90–140 Å in the closed state.
source: We generated a model of the open and closed states of M2β 15HPZ.GFP and found that the predicted distance between the active site of the free head (FH) and its C-terminal GFP tag is about 90–140 Å, assuming the GFP tags are flexibly linked to the tail, which is close enough to participate in FRET.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 1.

claim: All other donor-acceptor pairs (blocked head [BH] to either C-terminal GFP tag, FH to the BH C-terminal GFP) have distances ~130–140 Å in the closed state.
source: All other donor-acceptor pairs (blocked head [BH] to either C-terminal GFP tag, FH to the BH C-terminal GFP) have distances ~130–140 Å (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 1.

claim: The distance in the open state is predicted to be ≥250 Å, which is too far to participate in FRET.
source: In contrast, the distance in the open state is predicted to be ≥250 Å, which is much too far to participate in FRET.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 1.

claim: The FRET biosensor would be able to detect the IHM formation in solution.
source: Therefore, we proposed that the FRET biosensor would be able to detect the IHM formation in solution and that the FRET distance observed would be an ensemble average of all donor acceptor pairs, which are in the range of 90–140 Å apart in the IHM.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the FRET biosensor design.

claim: The WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP preparations were >95% pure based on SDS-PAGE.
source: The WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP preparations were >95% pure based on SDS-PAGE and similar in purity to our M2β S1 preparations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ATPase activity per head was similar when comparing WT S1 to WT 15HPZ.GFP (4.24±0.09 and 4.14±0.08 s–1, respectively).
source: The ATPase activity per head was similar when comparing WT S1 to WT 15HPZ.GFP (4.24±0.09 and 4.14±0.08 s–1, respectively) and E525K S1 to E525K 15HPZ.GFP (5.03±0.09 and 4.93±0.03 s–1, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by NH4+ ATPase assay data.

claim: E525K displayed a 20% higher NH4+ ATPase rate in both the S1 and 15HPZ.GFP preparations.
source: However, E525K displayed a 20% higher NH4+ ATPase rate in both the S1 and 15HPZ.GFP preparations.
evidence: This claim is supported by NH4+ ATPase assay data.

claim: The M2β 15HPZ.GFP construct does not disrupt the folding of the myosin motor domain.
source: Our NH4+ ATPase and SDS-PAGE results demonstrate that the M2β 15HPZ.GFP construct does not disrupt the folding of the myosin motor domain.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the NH4+ ATPase and SDS-PAGE data.

claim: The maximum actin-activated ATPase activity (kcat) of WT M2β 15HPZ.GFP was reduced sevenfold compared to WT M2β S1.
source: The maximum actin-activated ATPase activity (kcat) of WT M2β 15HPZ.GFP was reduced sevenfold compared to our measurements with WT M2β S1 (Tang et al., 2021), while the actin concentration at which the ATPase activity is one-half maximal (KATPase) was not significantly different in low-salt conditions (20 mM KCl; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by actin-activated ATPase data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: The actin concentration at which the ATPase activity is one-half maximal (KATPase) was not significantly different between WT M2β 15HPZ.GFP and WT M2β S1 in low-salt conditions (20 mM KCl).
source: The maximum actin-activated ATPase activity (kcat) of WT M2β 15HPZ.GFP was reduced sevenfold compared to our measurements with WT M2β S1 (Tang et al., 2021), while the actin concentration at which the ATPase activity is one-half maximal (KATPase) was not significantly different in low-salt conditions (20 mM KCl; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by actin-activated ATPase data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: In the WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP constructs, the kcat and KATPase were not significantly different.
source: In the WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP constructs, the kcat and KATPase were not significantly different.
evidence: This claim is supported by actin-activated ATPase data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: The E525K mutation increases kcat 20% and dramatically reduces the KATPase 30-fold in S1 constructs.
source: To our surprise, we found that the mutation increases kcat 20% and dramatically reduces the KATPase 30-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by actin-activated ATPase data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The E525K mutation enhances catalytic efficiency in S1.
source: Thus, the E525K mutation enhances catalytic efficiency in S1, but the SRX state is still able to suppress actin-activated ATPase activity in the double-headed HMM construct.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the actin-activated ATPase data.

claim: The SRX state is still able to suppress actin-activated ATPase activity in the double-headed HMM construct despite the E525K mutation enhancing catalytic efficiency in S1.
source: Thus, the E525K mutation enhances catalytic efficiency in S1, but the SRX state is still able to suppress actin-activated ATPase activity in the double-headed HMM construct.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the actin-activated ATPase data comparing S1 and HMM.

claim: The average in vitro gliding velocity was similar in WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP.
source: We also performed in vitro gliding assays and found that the average in vitro gliding velocity was similar in WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP (Figure 2C and Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro motility data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The velocities in HMM were similar to previous reports with a longer HMM construct but slower than published results with S1.
source: The velocities were similar to previous reports with a longer HMM construct (Winkelmann et al., 2015) but slower than our published results with S1 (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited previous studies.

claim: There was a larger number of stuck filaments in HMM experiments compared to S1.
source: There was a larger number of stuck filaments in our HMM experiments compared to S1 (Table 1), suggesting that myosin in the auto-inhibited SRX state may adopt a conformation on the motility surface that can bind actin and generate a drag force that opposes the filament sliding.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro motility data shown in Table 1.

claim: Myosin in the auto-inhibited SRX state may adopt a conformation on the motility surface that can bind actin and generate a drag force that opposes the filament sliding.
source: There was a larger number of stuck filaments in our HMM experiments compared to S1 (Table 1), suggesting that myosin in the auto-inhibited SRX state may adopt a conformation on the motility surface that can bind actin and generate a drag force that opposes the filament sliding.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the stuck filament data.

claim: Cardiac myosin exhibits two phases in single turnover measurements, a fast phase that is similar to the basal ATPase rate of S1 and a slow phase that is 5–10-fold slower and referred to as the SRX state.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that cardiac myosin exhibits two phases in single turnover measurements, a fast phase that is similar to the basal ATPase rate of S1 and a slow phase that is 5–10-fold slower and referred to as the SRX state (Anderson et al., 2018; Hooijman et al., 2011; Rohde et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: KCl destabilizes the SRX state in WT M2β 15HPZ.GFP, becoming a minor component at 150 mM KCl.
source: We performed single turnover measurements at various KCl concentrations and observed that KCl destabilizes the SRX state in WT M2β 15HPZ.GFP, becoming a minor component at 150 mM KCl (Figure 3A, C–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by single turnover data shown in Figure 3.

claim: E525K exhibited a much higher fraction of molecules in the SRX state compared to WT, especially at higher KCl concentrations.
source: However, E525K exhibited a much higher fraction of molecules in the SRX state compared to WT, especially at higher KCl concentrations (Figure 3B, C-figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by single turnover data shown in Figure 3.

claim: E525K stabilizes the SRX state even under physiological ionic strength conditions.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate E525K stabilizes the SRX state even under physiological ionic strength conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on the single turnover data at various KCl concentrations.

claim: The observed rate constants for the fast and slow components of the transients were relatively similar (~within twofold) in WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP.
source: The observed rate constants for the fast and slow components of the transients were relatively similar (~within twofold) in WT and E525K M2β 15HPZ.GFP (Figure 3D and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by single turnover data shown in Figure 3D and Table 2.

claim: The slow phase that represents the SRX state was a small fraction of the fluorescence transients (~5%) in M2β S1, was similar in WT and E525K, and was independent of ionic strength.
source: We also monitored the mantATP single turnover rate constants in WT and E525K M2β S1. We found that the slow phase that represents the SRX state was a small fraction of the fluorescence transients (~5%), was similar in WT and E525K, and was independent of ionic strength (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by single turnover data for S1 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Table 3.

claim: The rate constants of the SRX and DRX states were two- to fourfold faster in E525K compared to WT M2β S1.
source: The rate constants of the SRX and DRX states were two- to fourfold faster in E525K compared to WT M2β S1 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by single turnover data for S1 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Table 3.

claim: The rate constants for the DRX state were faster for S1 compared to 15HPZ.GFP in both WT and E525K.
source: The rate constants for the DRX state were faster for S1 compared to 15HPZ.GFP in both WT and E525K, while only the mutant also had a faster SRX rate constant in S1 compared to 15HPZ.GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of single turnover data for S1 and HMM shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The results demonstrate a larger increase in DRX rates for S1 constructs compared to 15HPZ.GFP than previously reported by Rohde et al., 2018 in proteolytically prepared bovine cardiac HMM.
source: Our results demonstrate a larger increase in DRX rates for S1 constructs compared to 15HPZ.GFP than previously reported by Rohde et al., 2018 in proteolytically prepared bovine cardiac HMM.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison to a cited previous study.

claim: Donor quenching was observed at low salt (5–10%) in the presence of the acceptor that was attenuated at high salt.
source: We observed donor quenching at low salt (5–10%) in the presence of the acceptor that was attenuated at high salt and a similar trend by monitoring acceptor enhancement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence emission spectra data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FRET transients clearly demonstrated donor quenching in the presence of the acceptor, while donor only controls exhibited no change in fluorescence.
source: The FRET transients clearly demonstrated donor quenching in the presence of the acceptor, while donor only controls exhibited no change in fluorescence (Figure 4A&B).
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow FRET data shown in Figure 4.

claim: WT had a smaller total amplitude at high salt (150 mM) compared to low salt (20 mM) in FRET experiments.
source: We plotted the total amplitude of the FRET change upon Cy3ATP binding as a function of Cy3ATP concentration and found that WT had a smaller total amplitude at high salt (150 mM) compared to low salt (20 mM; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow FRET data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The total amplitudes with the E525K experiments were quite insensitive to KCl concentration, suggesting more M2β 15HPZ.GFP molecules were in the IHM conformation at higher salt.
source: However, the total amplitudes with the E525K experiments were quite insensitive to KCl concentration (Figure 4D), suggesting more M2β 15HPZ.GFP molecules were in the IHM conformation at higher salt.
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow FRET data shown in Figure 4D and inference from the data.

claim: All of the rate constants were linearly dependent on Cy3ATP concentration.
source: All of the rate constants were linearly dependent on Cy3ATP concentration (Figure 4E and F), suggesting they represent second-order rate constants for ATP binding (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow FRET data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The rate constants represent second-order rate constants for ATP binding.
source: All of the rate constants were linearly dependent on Cy3ATP concentration (Figure 4E and F), suggesting they represent second-order rate constants for ATP binding (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the linear dependence of rate constants on Cy3ATP concentration.

claim: The relative amplitude of the fast phase was higher in WT (65%) than E525K (25%) at low salt.
source: The relative amplitude of the fast phase was higher in WT (65%) than E525K (25%) at low salt (Table 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow FRET data shown in Table 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The IHM FRET experiments followed a similar trend compared to the single ATP turnover experiments.
source: Overall, the IHM FRET experiments followed a similar trend compared to the single ATP turnover experiments, suggesting the SRX biochemical state correlates with the IHM structural state.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of FRET and single turnover data.

claim: WT shifts to a lower FRET state at higher KCl concentrations, while E525K maintains a similar FRET efficiency at low and high salt.
source: We measured the FRET efficiency (0.25 µM M2β and 1 µM Cy3ATP) as a function of KCl concentration and found that WT shifts to a lower FRET state at higher KCl concentrations, while E525K maintains a similar FRET efficiency at low and high salt (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by steady-state FRET data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The expected FRET efficiencies followed a similar trend to the measured efficiencies, especially in the E525K mutant.
source: The expected FRET efficiencies followed a similar trend to the measured efficiencies, especially in the E525K mutant, while the largest discrepancies were observed with WT in higher salt conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of measured and predicted FRET efficiencies shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The largest discrepancies between expected and measured FRET efficiencies were observed with WT in higher salt conditions, likely due to the greater degree of uncertainty with the measurements at high salt.
source: The expected FRET efficiencies followed a similar trend to the measured efficiencies, especially in the E525K mutant, while the largest discrepancies were observed with WT in higher salt conditions. This is likely due to the greater degree of uncertainty with the measurements at high salt, which contained the lowest FRET efficiencies.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparison of measured and predicted FRET efficiencies.

claim: Time-resolved FRET measurements resulted in very similar FRET efficiencies to steady-state FRET measurements.
source: Overall, we found that the time-resolved and steady-state FRET measurements resulted in very similar FRET efficiencies (Figure 5A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of time-resolved and steady-state FRET data shown in Figure 5.

claim: WT molecules were dominated by non-interacting heads, producing an 'open' conformation, with only a small number of 'closed' (folded) IHM structures.
source: WT molecules were dominated by non-interacting heads, producing an 'open' conformation (Figure 6A, yellow circles; Figure 6D), with only a small number of 'closed' (folded) IHM structures (Figure 6A, green circles; Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 6.

claim: More of the E525K molecules adopted the folded (IHM) conformation compared to WT.
source: In contrast, more of the E525K molecules adopted the folded (IHM) conformation (Figure 6B, green circles; Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was a clear and dramatic 3-4 fold increase in the number of closed conformations in E525K compared with WT.
source: Despite the experimental 'noise' introduced by these factors, there was a clear and dramatic 3-4 fold increase in the number of closed conformations in E525K compared with WT, consistent with stabilization of the IHM by the mutation and with the FRET data (Figure 6D, Table 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by negative stain EM data shown in Figure 6D and Table 5.

claim: The IHM is easily disrupted by binding to the grid surface during specimen preparation.
source: Because the IHM is easily disrupted by binding to the grid surface during specimen preparation (Burgess et al., 2007), we examined the molecules in low-salt (20 mM KCl) conditions, which strengthen the IHM, and minimized the time of contact of protein with the grid before staining.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The 2D class averages clearly show that in the case of E525K, more of the molecules form the IHM conformation when compared with WT.
source: The class averages clearly show that in the case of E525K, more of the molecules form the IHM conformation when compared with WT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D class averaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The E525K class average reveals key features of the IHM, including the BHs and FHs, the two light chains (essential light chains, ELCs, and regulatory light chains, RLCs), and sub-fragment 2 interacting with the BH.
source: The E525K class average shown in Figure 6C reveals key features of the IHM, including the BHs and FHs, the two light chains (essential light chains, ELCs, and regulatory light chains, RLCs), and sub-fragment 2 interacting with the BH, all well-documented features of the IHM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by 2D class averaging data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The raw EM images and the 2D class averages qualitatively support the ATP turnover and FRET results showing that E525K promotes the IHM and thus stabilizes the SRX state.
source: We conclude that the raw EM images and the 2D class averages qualitatively support our ATP turnover and FRET results showing that E525K promotes the IHM and thus stabilizes the SRX state.
evidence: This claim is based on integration of EM, FRET, and single turnover data.
